name: Colin Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Thornley Farm for the Ashworth family, who own it but live in the city. It's 300 hectares: 250 beef cattle finishing in the yards, plus oilseed rape and wheat. Mornings I'm round the cattle with Dean, one of my two staff, then I'm in the office doing the grain sales, the feed orders and the rota. I'd say it's half boots, half desk these days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the variety, a bit of everything and nobody watching me. What wears me out is the monthly report for the Ashworths, which takes me two evenings. I've started using one of the AI chat tools to summarise grain market news now and then, once I saw my neighbour doing it, and it's decent. My wife Anne does bookkeeping for six local farms part-time, so between us we know where every penny goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, like most things. At the discussion group I'd say it's handy for some bits and leave it there. I'm not one for big opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things stay as they are, and they're good. The job pays well, we live in the farm cottage, and we've got our own house in the village rented out plus decent savings. I'd be comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep managing Thornley the way I do. Keep using the AI for the market news and maybe the monthly report. Nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable. Maybe a bit relieved for Anne's sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why relieved for Anne?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Anne's bookkeeping is all screens and numbers, the kind of work I'd always thought would be first in line. If AI stays a gadget, her six farms stay hers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the time saved change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might shave an evening off the Ashworth report, which would be nice. I'd use the extra evening at the pub quiz, which we never win.

I'd keep my **opinions** for the discussion group, not online.
think: Things stay as they are, and they're **good**.
With the **village house** rented out and savings, I'd be comfortable.
do: Keep **managing Thornley** the way he does now.
Keep using AI for **market news** and maybe the monthly report.
feel: **Comfortable**, and a bit relieved for **Anne's** bookkeeping work.

The household's exposure sits mainly with **Anne's bookkeeping**.

steps.text: Keep managing the cattle, grain sales and rota at Thornley
Use the AI tool to draft the monthly Ashworth report

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that use it sensibly will do fine, and those that don't will fall behind. At the discussion group I'd say let's see who gets good results and copy them. Same as with every new bit of kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it touches me more than most farmers. Half my job is the desk side: grain sales, feed buying, planning, the report. If software does that, the Ashworths might ask why they pay a manager rather than a good stockman. And Anne's bookkeeping clients would start using AI instead of her, so our income could drop on both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get properly good at the AI tools, so I'm the one running them, not the one replaced by them. I'd go to the Ashworths before they come to me and offer to take on the neighbouring farm they've been eyeing, using the time AI saves. Anne and I would stop spending the rent from the village house and bank it instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd rather be doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the Ashworths?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: you've got a manager who already uses AI and knows every field. With the time it saves, I can run Thornley and the Brierley land they want to buy. A farm manager who uses AI can run more hectares, which makes me cheaper per hectare, not surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Anne do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anne would say she's 57 and not starting again. She might keep her two biggest clients and let the rest go. We'd lose maybe a third of her income, which we can stand, but she'd feel it more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too quick for anyone to handle well and the government needs to slow it down or cushion it. I'm not usually one for that. But two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be out in about 2029. If AGI can plan, buy and sell better than me by 2028, the Ashworths would keep Dean for the cattle and run the rest from their laptop in the city. Then around 2031 the robots come for Dean too. And the cottage goes with the job, so we'd lose our home as well as my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd tell our tenants in the village house we'll need it back within two years, so we have somewhere to go. I'd save everything we can and not touch the savings. Once AGI arrives, I'd look for a hands-on job, a herdsman's post on a big beef unit, because that's safe until the robots, three more years. At 60, three years of good wages gets me close enough to retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Losing a job is one thing, but losing the farm cottage at the same time is another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you spend those two years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nights would be spent doing spreadsheets on whether 63 is old enough to stop. Probably with an AI helping me, which is a bit rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Anne's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anne's clients would go fast too. So for a year or two we might have no earned income at all, just rent and savings. We'd manage, but I wouldn't sleep.

say: It's **too quick** for anyone to handle well.
Government should **slow it down** or cushion it, which isn't like me.
think: I'd be **out by 2029** once AGI can plan, buy and sell.
The **cottage** goes with the job, so we'd lose our home too.
do: Give the village house tenants **notice** to take it back.
Save everything and **don't touch** the savings.
Take a **herdsman's job** on a beef unit until the robots come.
feel: **Alarmed**, mainly about losing the **cottage** with the job.

fieldNote: The thinking side of his job goes in **2028**, three years before the hands-on part.
Plans to **move to hands-on work** to ride out the gap until the robots.

steps.text: Give the village house tenants notice so the family can move back in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and anyone who's caught out has only themselves partly to blame. Partly. At the discussion group I'd say start learning the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the dates almost work. AGI in 2031, when I'm 63, and robots around 2034. I'd likely lose the desk half of my job in 2031, but I could stay on as a working stockman for three years and retire at about 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the five years becoming the person on Thornley who runs the AI, so I'm useful longer. I'd agree a deal with the Ashworths now: if the manager role goes, I step down to herdsman and keep the cottage until 2034. And Anne and I would wait to see what her clients do before she makes any decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, about the cottage, but less. There's a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the Ashworths agree to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for it in writing. Old Mr Ashworth is fair, but his son runs things now and I don't know him well. A paper promise matters more with the son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather keep the title or keep the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house, every time. I'd take the drop in pay to stay in the farm cottage, because pride's cheaper than rent.

Anyone caught out is **partly** to blame, but only partly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and good farms will be fine. It's the same message as usual, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's after I've stopped. I'd retire at about 64, in 2032, before AGI even arrives. It's the next manager's problem, and maybe Dean's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on managing Thornley and bring retirement forward a couple of years, since the house and savings would allow it. I'd keep using AI tools as they improve. And I'd help Dean think about what he does in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. There's the usual background worry about Anne's clients and the Ashworth son, but it's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Dean. What would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dean's 40. By 2039 he'd be 53, too young to stop, too old to start fresh. I'd tell him to learn the robots. Someone has to fix the farm robots in a muddy yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Anne?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anne's clients would probably drift to AI over these ten years anyway. She'd likely retire with me in 2032. We'd travel a bit, and I'd do relief work on farms when I got bored.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the desk half of my job goes first and the cottage goes with it. What would help is a rule that a farm worker in tied housing gets proper notice, at least a year, and help with rehousing. Tied cottages are a trap nobody talks about.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about managers. Everyone pictures farmers as all boots, but a lot of us are half office now. The AI part of these pictures hits us first.

headlineQuote: Everyone pictures farmers as all boots, but a lot of us are half office now.
portrait: A 58-year-old **farm manager** running Thornley for the absentee Ashworth family.

Lives in a **tied cottage** and owns a rented-out house in the village.

Calm when AI stalls, **alarmed** by AGI in 2028, settled with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the desk half of his job and the cottage go together.
whatWouldHelp: At least **a year's notice** and rehousing help for workers in tied housing.
